item.title: REVIEW: TP-Link Archer BE600 Review: Multi-Gig Speed, But Needs Greater Reach
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Designed for people who need 10Gbps WAN connectivity, the TP-Link Archer BE600 ($249.99) is a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router that offers five multi-gig networking ports (including a 10Gbps WAN/LAN port) and 6GHz wireless transmissions. It comes with TP-Link’s HomeShield software, with many of its parental control and network security features hidden behind a paywall. The BE600 turned in fast scores on our throughput performance tests, but its signal strength performance was less than stellar. If you're looking for a Wi-Fi 7 router with gamer-friendly features that delivers strong 2.4GHz and 5GHz Wi-Fi to every corner of your home, the $279.99 Editors’ Choice-winning TP-Link Archer GE650 is a better choice. The BE600 looks nothing like the volcano-inspired GE650 router. Instead, it uses a traditional black desktop enclosure that measures 1.8 by 10 by 5.5 inches (HWD) and sports six external adjustable antennas. The textured top of the router contains tiny LED status indicators for power, each radio band, internet connectivity, LAN connectivity, and WPS activity. The back panel houses a 10Gbps WAN/LAN port, a 2.5Gbps WAN/LAN port, and three 2.5Gbps LAN ports. They share space with the WPS, Reset, and Power buttons, as well as a power jack. A single Type-A USB 3.0 port is on the right side of the router. The BE600 uses a 2.0GHz quad-core processor, 1GB of DDR4 RAM, and 256MB of flash memory. It can hit maximum data rates of up to 1,032Mbps on the 2.4GHz band, up to 2,882Mbps on the 5GHz band, and up to 5,765Mbps on the 6GHz band, for a total combined throughput of 9.7Gbps (hence its BE9700 designation, where "BE" is the version identifier for Wi-Fi 7). It uses all of the latest Wi-Fi 7 technologies, including orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA) transmissions, 320MHz channel bandwidth, Multi-Link Operation (MLO), 4K QAM, direct-to-client beamforming, and MU-MIMO data streaming. It also supports TP-Link’s EasyMesh technology, which means it can serve as a main router or a mesh node alongside other TP-Link EasyMesh-compatible devices. As with all TP-Link routers, the BE600 can be managed via a web-based interface or the company’s Tether mobile app for iOS and Android devices. The Tether app’s Network screen displays a picture of the router, its current status, and real-time upload and download speeds. Below the speed reading are tabs labeled Network Status, Clients, Traffic Usage, and Guest Network. When you tap the Network Status panel, you'll see a screen with CPU and memory usage charts, upload and download speeds, and router information such as the model number, the MAC and IP addresses, and the firmware version. To see a list of online and offline devices, tap the Clients panel. Here you can view upload and download data and view a traffic usage chart for each client, see when the client joined the network, set speed limits, and give the client bandwidth priority. Tapping the Traffic Usage panel is similar, as it lets you view upload and download speed charts for each client. The Guest network panel lets you create a separate SSID for guests, allowing them to browse the internet without access to the main network. At the very bottom of the Network screen are Network, Security, Family, and More buttons. The Network button takes you back to the Network screen from anywhere in the app, and the Security button opens a screen where you can scan the network for router, wireless, and encryption security risks. For more advanced security features, you can subscribe to the $4.99 monthly ($35.99 yearly) HomeShield Security+ plan, which includes Web Protection against malicious sites, Intrusion Prevention against external attacks, and IoT Protection for your smart home devices. TP-Link’s Total Security package, which costs $5.99 per month ($69.99 yearly), adds antivirus protection, a VPN service, password management, and PC cleaning tools. The Family button opens a screen where you can create user profiles, apply age-based website filters, filter content, and create bedtime schedules. Advanced controls such as SafeSearch content filtering, Time Limits that let you set a daily cap on online time, and YouTube restrictions cost another $2.99 per month, or $17.99 per year. Tap the More button to access Wi-Fi and QoS settings, enable Eco mode (adjusts power consumption based on real-time traffic usage), set up a mesh network, optimize the network, run network diagnostics, and configure VPS client and server settings. Advanced settings include Port Forwarding, Port Triggering, Static Routing, Device Isolation, and Firewall settings. Installing the BE600 is fast and easy, whether you use the Tether app or the web console. I used the Tether app. First, I unplugged my modem and connected it to the router’s 10Gbps WAN port, then powered up both devices. I opened the Tether app, tapped Add Device, tapped Standard Routers, and scanned the QR code on the bottom of the router when prompted. After several seconds, the app recognized the router, so I tapped Set Up This Device and created a management password. Next, I created a network name and password for the 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz bands, and within a minute the new network was created and ready for testing. Bingo. The BE600 had a solid showing on our throughput performance tests. Its score of 212Mbps on the 2.4GHz close proximity test was better than the TP-Link Archer GE800 (195Mbps) and the Asus RT-BE96U (150Mbps) but couldn’t keep pace with the Archer GE650 (246Mbps). On the 30-foot test, the BE600 trailed the pack (if only slightly) with a score of 80Mbps. The Archer GE800 and Archer GE650 both scored 86Mbps, and the Asus RT-BE96U scored 83Mbps. The BE600’s score of 1,885Mbps on the 5GHz close proximity test was faster than the Asus RT-BE96U (1,548Mbps) but trailed the Archer GE800 (1,989Mbps) and the Archer GE650 (2,131Mbps). Its score of 642Mbps on the 30-foot test was significantly slower than that of the Archer GE800 (736Mbps), the RT-BE96U (906Mbps), and the Archer GE650 (788Mbps). Throughput speeds on the 6GHz band were also respectable, generally just slightly behind this pack. The BE600 managed 2,314Mbps on the close proximity test and 280Mbps on the 30-foot test. The Archer GE800 scored 2,337Mbps (close proximity) and 338Mbps (30 feet); the Asus RT-BE96U scored 2,451Mbps and 311Mbps, respectively; and the Archer GE650 scored 2,334Mbps and 316Mbps, respectively. To test wireless signal strength, we used Ekahau’s Sidekick 2 Wi-Fi diagnostic device and its Survey mobile app. This combo generates heat maps that display the router's 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz signal strength throughout our test home. The white circle on the map represents the router's location, and the colors indicate signal strength. Dark greens depict the strongest signal, yellows represent a weaker signal, and grays indicate a very weak or nonexistent signal. As shown on the maps below, the BE600 was unable to deliver strong signals throughout the house. Its 2.4GHz coverage was weak in parts of the garage and back bedroom, and it had trouble delivering a strong 5GHz signal strength in most of the garage, the den, and the dining room. Its 6GHz signal strength was even worse, but on par with other 6GHz routers we’ve tested due to Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) power limitations. To test file transfer performance, we measure read and write speeds by moving a 1.5GB folder containing photos, videos, music, and office documents back and forth between a USB 3.0 drive connected to the router and our desktop PC, which is also connected to the router. The BE600 turned in respectable scores here (80MBps on both tests), but they were not quite as fast as the competition. The Archer GE800 scored 87MBps (write) and 84MBps (read), the Asus RT-BE96U scored 82MBps (write) and 83MBps (read), and the Archer GE650 scored 85MBps on both tests. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. If you want to make the most of your gigabit-plus internet service, the TP-Link Archer BE600 BE9700 Tri-Band Wi-Fi 7 Router has your back. It offers several high-speed networking ports, including a 10Gbps WAN/LAN port and four 2.5Gbps LAN ports. It also supports 6GHz transmissions, and it comes with basic parental control and network security software. While the BE600 turned in solid scores on our throughput tests, its signal range performance was questionable. At $249.99, the BE600 won’t break the bank, but for around $30 more, the TP-Link Archer GE650 offers better all-around performance, as well as additional gamer-friendly features and settings. It remains our top pick for midrange Wi-Fi 7 routers. I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: SALES: 10 travel gifts I swear by after 17 years traveling with kids
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Speaking as someone who is now approaching 17 years of experience traveling with kids, having the right "stuff" matters more than you might think. Something for the kids to do, something to keep the devices charged, something to hold all the stuff, something to hold the kid and something comfy to wear (with pockets!) throughout the process are just a few of the things that can make family travel a little easier along the way. So, as we approach the holiday season, here are 11 of my tried-and-true recommendations for gifts, whether you're shopping for yourself or another family on the go. Best for: Preschool-aged kids who fly frequently If your family travels a lot and your preschool-aged kid wants a really cool piece of luggage all their own that matches yours, then the Away Kids Carry-On Luggage is a great choice. It's not only fun, but really well made. It comes in colors such as berry pink and dragonfly blue — and there are even some limited-edition colors and collections, including a current Toy Story line. The handle adjusts to two heights: one for them and one for you when they ... decide to be done. Like the full-size models, it has a TSA-approved lock and a compression system. Once your kiddos get much past the preschool years, they might be better off with full-sized Away Carry-On bags simply because they hold more. But there are a few good years when these bags are absolutely perfect for little frequent flyers. TPG tip: Not only does Away sometimes run pretty decent Black Friday sales, but there are periodically Chase Offers that save you $50 or more on certain Away bag orders with cards such as the (see rates and fees). Best for: Families with multiple devices they need to keep charged on the go Phones, tablets, headphones — virtually everything requires power on the go these days, so having a good charger for the family is a must. Anker makes some of the best, and one that can be especially handy when you have a family's worth of devices to keep charged is the Anker MagGo Power Bank. It has a kickstand, shows you the battery percentage and time remaining to charge, can charge itself while recharging your devices and can get an iPhone to about 50% power in just 30 minutes. TPG tip: Anker chargers are sold at many big retailers, so to earn bonus miles or cash back on this (and other) purchases, check CashBackMonitor.com before buying to see which shopping portal is offering the biggest reward for clicking through first. Best for: Teens and tweens who like taking pictures and having something tangible to show for it beyond photos on their phones Gen Alpha and Gen Z are into nostalgia — and with that comes photos you can hold in your hand instead of just viewing on your phone. Frankly, I'm here for it. One of the mini cameras that makes this easy is the Fujifilm Instax Mini 13. It has two self-timer options, a cute design available in five colors and produces instant prints measuring roughly 2 by 3 inches. It's a fun way to give your kids physical memories of their travels instead of having every photo live somewhere in the cloud. TPG tip: The camera typically does not come with film, so be sure to pick up Instax mini instant film to go with the gift. Best for: Moms who want to be comfy on the plane but also a tiny bit on trend Being comfortable when kiddos are involved is often priority number one, whether you're running around at home, navigating an airport or flying halfway around the world. Enter one of my favorite brands: Vuori, which makes some of the most comfortable clothes I own. My current favorite is the Vuori Halo Essential Wide Leg Pants in black. They go with almost everything, are cozy for the plane, are made with Vuori's DreamKnit material and have pockets — an absolute must on travel days. They also come in short, regular and long lengths, so you can find the right fit. TPG tip: If you want even more comfy athleisure in your luggage or under the tree, remember that the comes with a quarterly up to $75 credit for Lululemon (enrollment required). And you can still check to see if Lululemon is on a site such as Rakuten to potentially earn some bonus points or cash back. Best for: Ages 3 - 10 often love these, but they can really work for virtually any age who likes to hold a 'pen' and draw. LCD drawing tablets are the definition of punching above their weight (er, price) class when it comes to how much entertainment they provide for how little they cost. We've had tablets like these draw a crowd at a delayed boarding gate full of children before, especially when Grandma was smart enough to buy a few extras "just in case" since they are so affordable. They're fun, mess-free, inexpensive and perfect for long flights or car rides. Plus, many are designed to be resistant to some inevitable drops and spills that come with traveling with kids. TPG tip: Because they are so affordable, it might be worth picking up an extra one. Best for: Travelers who want to stay organized (honestly, I think everyone who travels can benefit from these) The list of reasons I recommend packing cubes for family travel is longer than The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King extended edition. But here's the abridged version: You can easily pack by person or by day, stay organized and often fit more into your bags than you could without packing cubes. And a bonus reason I bet you wouldn't have guessed is that packing cubes can be a good way to help reduce the chances of bringing bed bugs home if you use them in your larger packing and unpacking strategy, as I do. Calpak makes very durable packing cubes that also come in really cute patterns and colors, such as polka dot and dark cherry, alongside classics like black. TPG tip: Even if you don't pack for the whole trip by day, having a packing cube full of the first night and next full day's worth of clothes so you don't have to dig through all the bags right away is one of my favorite travel hacks. Best for: Anyone with Apple devices who owns virtually anything they don't want to lose. At this point, we probably almost all know and love AirTags. But with the second generation now offering improved range, they're even more useful, and honestly, I don't think you can realistically ever have too many. Put one in each piece of luggage, your kids' backpacks, your sling bag, on your keychain, on your pet's collar, even in your carry-on bags you don't plan to be parted from ... just in case. TPG tip: You can now share the location of the AirTag you put in your checked luggage with many airlines in case your bag is delayed, helping reunite you with your things faster. Best for: Travelers who want a sleek, cool, functional bag that looks like it cost a lot more than it did. I have luggage brands that cost double or more what this Quince bag costs, but it was just as light as those pricier brands I've tried and rolled at least as well with its 360° spinner wheels, had a very smooth and easy-to-use handle and came in a fun dark green color. TPG tip: The Quince expandable carry-on is the one I was gifted by Quince to try out, and I love the extra space over the traditional carry-on size and it fit in the overhead bin just fine. However, be aware that some airlines (and certain gate agents) can be stricter than others about size limits on expandable luggage and may ask you to unexpand it. Best for: Families with newborns and young babies When I look back on our time with little kids, there's one purchase that I'd make a million times over: The Doona. And I still see parents-in-the-know using it now more than ever for the same reason we loved it once upon a time. The Doona transforms from a car seat into a stroller in seconds, without even having to take your baby out of the seat. It's fantastic for hopping in and out of cabs, navigating airports and bringing an approved car seat aboard a plane, all without having to lug both a car seat and a stroller. One caveat: It's rated for babies weighing 4 to 35 pounds and measuring up to 32 inches tall, but in my experience, it isn't uncommon for kids to outgrow it well before their first birthday. For those early months when it works, though, it's fantastic. TPG tip: You can typically fly with your Doona if you purchase your baby a seat, even though you typically don't have to have them in their own seat until they turn two. Best for: Parents who love to travel with kids ages 2 to 6 who weigh under 80 pounds There's an awkward phase of family travel when your kids might be too big for you to want to haul a stroller everywhere with you but still can't be trusted to walk through an airport at a reasonable pace for more than 30 seconds. And for that phase, having luggage that little kids can 'ride' on can be both handy and fun. One of the brands that offers that is Younglingz with their ride-on suitcases that come in fun themes like unicorns, fire trucks and motorcycles. This way, you are getting your kids and their things through the airport even when the walk starts to get a little longer than you'd like. TPG tip: If you are purchasing this (or anything) on Amazon, be on the lookout for periodic promotions that can save you $15 to $40 (or sometimes more) by using just a few Amex Membership Rewards points toward the purchase.

item.title: REVIEW: This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers
item.description:
Source: The Verge
As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con, my family and I can’t stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo’s Zero 2 controllers for games that don’t use analog thumbsticks. I’ve spent years hunting for an alternative that pairs the size of the Zero 2 with as much of the functionality of a larger controller as I can get, and CRKD’s new Atom Plus is nearly exactly that. But if you have larger hands like I do, you may find the gamepad’s focus on portability a struggle. This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers Larger hands may struggle with the Atom Plus, but it squeezes a lot of functionality into an extremely tiny controller. If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Measuring around 3.5 inches wide, the $29.99 Atom Plus is about a half-inch smaller than the 8BitDo Zero 2 but squeezes in considerably more features and functionality. The most obvious is a pair of symmetrical analog thumbsticks with anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance technology. You also get shoulder buttons and triggers, rumble feedback, a dedicated home button, motion controls, and customization through a mobile app. Like many third-party controllers, the Atom Plus works with multiple platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2, PCs, Android, iOS, and various smart TVs. And just like other gamepads, pairing to different devices requires putting the Atom Plus into one of several Bluetooth modes by holding down a combination of buttons at power-up, which in this case is the home button plus a specific direction on the D-pad. It’s easy to do, but never easy to remember: I frequently needed to grab the manual or quickly Google which direction I need to press when switching devices. The Atom Plus already features a bunch of technical info etched into the back of the controller, so I’d love to see these important pairing instructions included there, too. (And that goes for all multiplatform gamepads.) I primarily tested the Atom Plus with the Nintendo Switch 2 since I mostly plan to use the controller as a travel accessory. The thumbsticks are about the same size as those on the original Switch Joy-Con, which means they’re smaller than the Switch 2’s. And while I prefer an asymmetrical layout, the Atom Plus’ sticks are very good, with a little more tension than Nintendo’s that I find actually helps with precision movements given their limited travel. While the overall build quality feels excellent, the Atom Plus’ tiny footprint creates some compromises and challenges. The front action buttons and D-pad feel nice and squishy, but the gamepad’s controls are a little crowded. When pressing down or right on the D-pad, my thumb regularly bumps the left thumbstick. It doesn’t hinder gameplay, but I do find it an annoying distraction. The shoulder buttons use digital microswitches, as do the triggers, which means the latter can’t be used for racing games that support analog acceleration controls. I like that the two sets of buttons on the top edge sit at slightly different heights, but I would have preferred a little more differentiation since I’ve occasionally accidentally pressed the triggers when I meant to hit the shoulder buttons. I was impressed with the Atom Plus’ customizability, however. When paired to an accompanying mobile app, you can check the controller’s remaining charge, turn off rumble feedback, see its unique product number (by tapping your phone to an NFC chip inside the controller), and remap any of its controls. That includes the pair of dual-function shortcut levers that replicate the Switch’s plus and minus buttons and screenshot shortcut. Those levers move up and down and cleverly reduce the number of buttons crowding the front of the Atom Plus, but they feel a little too small, which is more or less the general theme. It’s a tiny gamepad that’s great for travel or stashing in your everyday carry. But, unsurprisingly, it probably won’t find its way into your regular gaming rotation. It’s assumed that players will be willing to settle for the compromise of occasionally contorting their fingers in weird, new ways for one of the smallest fully featured controllers on the market. I don’t think a dual-stick controller could get any smaller than the Atom Plus without making too many ergonomic compromises. So while I applaud CRKD for the careful balancing act behind the Atom Plus’ design, and would certainly recommend it for those wanting a very capable controller that’s also cheap and portable, I’m now curious how it compares to Microsoft’s recently announced Xbox Nano controller that’s “surprisingly comfortable,” according to The Verge’s Tom Warren. It’s $20 more expensive than CRKD’s and noticeably larger, but it adds analog triggers, a more spacious design, and stubby grips making it easier to hold for those of us with beefy mitts.

item.title: SALES: Stop Using Your Phone for Touch-Ups—This Travel Makeup Mirror Is Foldable and Lightweight
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
This past summer, my girlfriends and I packed our bags and headed to Rosemary Beach, Florida, for a bachelorette trip. Thirty minutes before landing, we collectively decided it was time for a quick refresh on the plane, pulling off our under-eye patches, applying lip liner, and attempting to tack on a little bit of makeup. I opened up my iPhone camera to guide me, but I could barely see what I was doing since the plane lights were off. You can imagine my surprise—and envy—when my best friend, Deanna, illuminated our row with her travel makeup mirror. It seemingly came out nowhere, and was already propped up on her seat tray, showing her exactly where she needed a touch-up. “I'm gonna need to borrow that,” I said. The pre-flight touch-up was not the only time Deanna's travel makeup mirror came in handy on our trip. One night before dinner, as 12 girls simultaneously got ready, she and I realized we were running short on bathroom mirrors. Rather than wait for the bathroom to clear and be forced to rush, or be late, we took turns doing our makeup with her travel mirror. Before we landed back at Newark Airport after the trip, I had already ordered Funtouch's travel makeup mirror for myself on Amazon. After a few months of having my own, I can honestly say this $17 travel accessory is worth every penny. While I initially envisioned using it on the plane or a crowded girls trip, it's proven handy on numerous occasions. Most recently, on a trip to Newport, Rhode Island, I pulled out my foldable travel mirror and did my makeup en-route. It was a relief to arrive at The Vanderbilt hotel looking and feeling put together, without having to sit through the whole four-hour car ride with a full face of makeup on first thing in the morning. It's very simple to use: Unfold the mirror to reveal its full size, then tap the touch-screen button in the center to turn on the light. It offers three different light settings, including white light (my favorite), warm light, and cool light. The same button turns the light off too. And if that's a little too much light, say on an early morning flight, you can long press the touch-screen button to dim the brightness level. Another perk: The mirror stands up on its own, so you don't have to worry about holding it or propping it up against anything. I love that the device is wireless. It comes with a USB charger so I can make sure it's powered up before I travel with it and leave the cord at home. The battery life is pretty impressive—I didn't need to recharge it after my four-day trip to Rhode Island. The portable device is also very slim—about the size of a Kindle or an iPad Mini—so it can be slipped into a tote bag, backpack, or weekender bag with ease. Its exterior is pretty durable too, so I don't need to worry about it getting crushed in my bag. Another thing I appreciate about this travel makeup mirror: no magnification—I don't need to see my pores that close! The mirror is just the right size to show you your full face, head, and neck without being bulky or heavy to travel with. It's lightweight, compact, and portable—the trifecta of any good travel accessory. If you're stumped on what to get someone you love this season, surprise them with something they'll actually use every time they travel. You might want to grab one for yourself too.

item.title: REVIEW: Lenovo Yoga Creative Keyboard Angry Miao Edition Review: Silence Is Golden, and Priced Like It
item.description:
Source: PCMag
My girlfriend hates my mechanical keyboards. Every one I’ve brought home, from clattery, clicky gaming models to boards sold as “quiet,” has earned a glare from across the room. Enter the Lenovo Yoga Creative Keyboard Angry Miao Edition: It's the first one she didn’t notice at all. Lenovo’s funky board is a collaboration with Angry Miao, a startup known for stylish product designs. Indeed, the Yoga Creative Keyboard ($299.99) is one of the most distinctive-looking keyboards ever to grace my desk. With a transparent frame and a huge control ring in the upper right corner, the Creative Keyboard truly stands out, and its deep sound dampening combined with near-silent key switches make it the quietest keyboard I’ve ever used. Still, while it's quirky and cool, its high price, limited customization options, weak ergonomics, and lack of wireless connectivity limit its appeal. If you're in the market for a general-use keyboard, the far cheaper and much more utilitarian Dell KB900 is our favorite everyday office keyboard, while the Editors' Choice-winning Razer Pro Type Ultra is our top premium pick. The Yoga Creative Keyboard is a full-layout keyboard, complete with a numeric keypad and a function row. It's compact for a full-size board, using a so-called "98%" layout, which means all the keys are there; they're just packed tighter than on a normal, full-size keyboard. It’s likely not enough of a difference to change the rhythm of your typing, and I commend Lenovo for trying to shrink the footprint as best it can. The keyboard measures 3.6 by 18.5 by 9.3 inches (HWD) and weighs a whopping 5.5 pounds, 2 pounds heavier than the Keychron K2 HE Concrete Edition—you know, the one actually made out of concrete! Needless to say, the keyboard’s frame is sturdy. Once it’s in place on your desk, moving it takes real effort. If you summon the strength to flip it over, you’ll see no retractable feet on the underside, which is not ideal for ergonomics. Adding them or including a detachable wrist rest would go a long way here. I don't expect a wrist rest to be included, but it would definitely sweeten the deal. Razer’s Tactile Orange key switches, found on boards like the BlackWidow 75% Pro, used to be my favorite, but I think they’ve finally been beaten by the Bsun Light Sakura Silent linear switches on the Yoga Creative Keyboard. With an actuation force of 37g, these switches feel ultra-light, a stark contrast to the solid frame they’re attached to. The keyboard uses "south-facing" LEDs beneath its keys. This variety of LED is positioned below the switch mechanism, shining downward, rather than above ("north-facing") and shining straight up through the keycap. South-facing LEDs tend to emit more diffuse, even light, and sometimes enable quieter operation since the LED isn't in the keycap's movement zone. I do wish the keycaps were translucent like the keyboard’s body, though, if only to better appreciate the RGB glow. As it stands now, you can barely notice the colors peeking out from under the keys. I’ve tested plenty of quiet mechanical keyboards, like the Corsair Vanguard Air 99 Wireless, and in each case I still notice a mild click-clack that emanates with every stroke. That’s why I was surprised at just how quiet the Creative Keyboard is. It’s so quiet that some may be thrown off by the lack of tactile feedback when typing. It’s as if you're not typing at all. The ultimate test, for me, as I noted up top, was typing in front of my girlfriend, who is irked by mechanical keyboards of all kinds. Against the odds, the Creative Keyboard was quiet enough to not bother her. And if it doesn’t bother her, chances are, it won’t disturb your neighbors in the office, either. On the contrary, if you're someone who wants more audible feedback from your keystrokes, you’ll be happy to know this board's switches are hot-swappable, so you can install third-party key switches that suit your preferences. But that wipes out one of the big reasons to buy it: the special Bsun switches. Still, it's not all about the switches. The lack of noise is also down to the keyboard’s multiple layers of sound dampening. Four foam cushion layers sandwich the keyboard’s printed circuit board (PCB), and two more Poron (a specialized type of foam) cushions are on top and bottom. And just like the multiple layers of a cake, these are baked into a gasket mount. All work together to contain any switch noise. Two downstream USB Type-C ports sit at the top of the keyboard, each offering 5Gbps throughput. The included USB cord, however, is extremely short, and the keyboard has no wireless connectivity available. The Creative Keyboard’s most distinctive feature, of course, is impossible to miss: the giant ring nestled in the keyboard’s right corner. Lenovo refers to it as both a dial and a Star Ring; we'll go with the latter. It is part volume roller, part workflow enhancer. Right below the ring, you’ll find a small switch with three positions. The left position maps the ring to volume control, the middle position maps it to the left and right arrow keys, and the right position maps it to Page Up and Page Down. This means the ring will take over any function that would normally be handled by arrow keys or page buttons. This ostensibly gives you more precision. For example, in video editing software, you can move the switch position to the middle and scrub through a timeline using the ring instead of the arrow keys. These are just some of the very basic use cases I can think of. I see a lot of potential here, especially for content creators. A Yoga key sits to the right of the function row and can be used to adjust lighting effects for both the Star Ring and the keys. Pressing the Yoga and Enter keys cycles through backlight colors for the switches, while pressing Yoga and the asterisk key (*) cycles through the same for the Star Ring. But that's all; the Yoga key exists just to manage the keyboard's RGB lighting. Lenovo confirmed to PCMag that this keyboard is essentially identical to Angry Miao's existing ATM 98 keyboard, with the only notable differences being the ATM 98's additional color options and the Lenovo version's Yoga key. As of this writing, the ATM 98 is $100 cheaper than the Yoga Creative Keyboard's list price. Now, Lenovo is hardly the first tech giant to rebadge a product from a smaller company. (See, for example, the OnePlus Keyboard 81 Pro, done in concert with Keychron, or the HyperX x Ducky One 2 Mini.) Still, a $100 premium for Lenovo branding is a big ask. True, you can find plenty of other keyboards in this price range. But most of them, such as the Corsair Vanguard Air 99 Wireless mentioned earlier, aim to justify their prices with extensive functionality or envelope-pushing technology that the Yoga Creative Keyboard lacks. Lenovo offers no dedicated software for the Yoga Creative Keyboard, and the company also confirmed it isn't QMK-compatible. QMK is an open-source firmware that runs directly on a keyboard's internal microcontroller. With QMK-compatible keyboards, you can program your own macros and remap keys, among other advanced features. While it's uncommon for big OEMs to support it (they usually have their own dedicated utilities), QMK is a darling in the custom keyboard scene. The ATM 98, by contrast, is a QMK board that works with the Via web app, which offers more robust software-based customization options. On that front, in a sense, you're paying less to get more. I do like the Lenovo Yoga Creative Keyboard, and I really wanted to love it. The typing feel is immaculate, the key switches are nearly silent, and the build quality is excellent. But the price, lack of customization software, muted RGB, and less-than-stellar ergonomics hold it back. The fact that the nearly identical ATM 98 is cheaper and more customizable is a further drawback. Ultimately, if you’re seeking a top-notch general-use keyboard, the Razer Pro Type Ultra is still one of our favorites. If you're drawn in by that giant ring to handle your creative workflows, the Yoga Creative Keyboard won’t disappoint, but you just might want to buy the ATM 98 instead. item.title: SALES: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is the game the Switch 2 was made for
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
The Nintendo Switch 2 hit shelves last year. But if Mario Kart World and Pokopia weren’t enough to sway you over to the handheld life, the latest Zelda installment may change your mind. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is the second remake of the 1998 N64 title by the same name. But this is by no means a straightforward port with a minor graphics upgrade (looking at you, Skyrim). This is a full revamp of a classic for the modern age – and no, you don’t need to have played the original to enjoy it. The sales speak for themselves, with over 5 million copies bought in the first four days of launch. But if you need a little more convincing, I’ve gone hands on with the game, exploring Hyrule in all its glory. Now I confess, I was a tad late to the Zelda party (I blame my past The Sims addiction taking most of my money). Breath of the Wild was my first taste of the franchise, but I’ve been playing this alongside my editorial assistant/husband who experienced the 2011 3DS version of Ocarina of Time. It’s been interesting to see our different perspectives. He’s able to compare how the mechanics and world have changed for the better. For example, the fact that time now passes in towns rather than just in the overworld, or that there’s finally a dedicated jump button. But perhaps his biggest source of amusement is seeing me experience everything for the first time, knowing what’s coming. For me, seeing how this Zelda universe differs to my beloved Breath of the Wild (seriously, I’ve got the tattoo to prove it) is intriguing. There’s more childhood wonder and whimsy in Ocarina of Time, meaning it’s a suitable title for the whole family. It also feels more linear and less sprawling… something very useful now I have less time on my hands as a new mom. While the Nintendo Switch 2 won’t exactly measure up to the latest and greatest gaming PCs on the graphics front, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time certainly pushes what this console is capable of with great levels of success. Playing it docked gives you the best view, with 4K HDR graphics at 60Hz (or 1440p at 120Hz, should you prefer). The world of Hyrule has an ethereal haze to it, with colors popping beautifully on the screen and dynamic shadows bringing the setting to life. Kokiri Forest is a particularly magical start to the game, with lush greens and twinkly lights that are so captivating, you won’t want to leave. This is the first game that has really exploited what this console is capable of compared to its predecessor. Now sure, going handheld isn’t quite as immersive, and those with a keen eye may notice a slight dip in quality with visuals in the far distance. Nonetheless, that large 7.9-inch screen will still impress when you’re looking to play on the go/from the comfort of your own bed. Nintendo’s hidden superpower is its music, and Ocarina of Time has a completely reimagined soundtrack with a belting orchestra. From the moment you boot it up for the first time, the opening music has you hooked. The developers have paid attention to the little details, with the sound transitioning beautifully between day and night in Kakariko Village. The voice acting in key scenes is also a wonderful touch carried over from the open-world games, along with the iconic/annoying commentary from Navi, depending on your preference. And less we forget there’s the interactive element with the Ocarina itself… though I’ll hold my thoughts on that for another piece. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is the game the Nintendo Switch 2 was made for. It’s beautiful to experience, a joy to ‘listen’ to and will appeal to all kinds of gamers. If you’re thinking about pulling the trigger on your first handheld console, now may be the time. Ocarina of Time is out now, and costs $59.99 for the digital version and $69.99 for the physical edition. The Switch 2 starts from $499.99.

Steve Jobs once said that customers don't know what they want until you show them. And he was right. Customers still may not know what they want, but if it's cheap enough, they'll buy it anyway and then throw it out and buy something else. There are two types of people: those who are aware of keyboard gunk and those who have blissfully never observed it. If we ever calculated how much time we've lost, as a species, to USB-related inconveniences, we would drag USB's creator before the ICC. item.title: SALES: The top 6 Nintendo Switch 2 exclusives of 2026

2026 has been huge for the Nintendo Switch 2. This year, it really feels like the console has come into its own, with a number of critically acclaimed first-party exclusives, as well as some heavy-hitting third-party titles that were beautifully optimized for the system (such as Resident Evil Requiem). Yes, the Switch 2’s library already feels surprisingly fleshed-out for a console that’s not even two years old yet, and it’s certainly become my main gaming device in 2026, squeezing more than 800 hours of playtime out of me. And looking back on the year as a whole got me thinking. What have been the best Nintendo Switch 2 games of 2026? Specifically, I want to look at exclusives here and run through the very best titles that have released since the dawn of the new year. I’ll be ranking my top six picks here, but if you have a different list, make sure to drop it in the comments! Before Yoshi and the Mysterious Book reared its whimsical head, I felt that our green dino was in something of a rut, with releases like Yoshi’s Wooly World and Crafted World failing to evoke the sense of wonder and thrill that the series conjured up in its youth. But all of that changed with Mysterious Book, which focused a lot more heavily on exploration, seeing Yoshi venture through the pages of the living Encyclopedia, Mr. E., in order to learn about the mysterious creatures that live within his pages. Thanks to this game’s stellar art direction, the pages come to life, both literally and figuratively speaking. The brilliant blend of beautiful 3D environments and hand-drawn watercolor-style characters results in a massively charming and immersive experience, with stop-motion animation giving each critter distinct, memorable personalities and traits. It’s not all about the visual style, though. Yoshi and the Mysterious Book is a blast from the moment you start playing until the credits roll, with no end of oddities to discover. While the game’s core puzzles are relatively straightforward, tracking down some of the collectibles is a genuine challenge — you’ll have to get creative with creature abilities and regularly stray from the beaten path in order to find secret areas and Smiley Flowers. While I would’ve liked to have seen some tougher boss battles and a bit more narrative depth from Yoshi and the Mysterious Book, it’s easily my favorite game that the series has produced in over a decade. I’ve still got so many secrets to uncover, and I’m looking forward to diving back in over the holidays. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is to the original Nintendo Switch Sports exactly what Wii Sports Resort was to Wii Sports. It brought more sports, more depth, and more replayability to the table, all while maintaining the simplicity that makes this series so beloved to gamers of all ages. Yes, I felt that the original Nintendo Switch Sports was seriously lacking in single-player content, had an underwhelming selection of events, and had a flawed points system, but all three of those woes were remedied in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. It truly feels like Nintendo took the time to listen to its audience, with a new Island Crown mode adding a competitive single-player edge, a grand total of 12 sports packed in, and the points system applied to both offline and online play, rather than just the latter. The core experience is great too. Every single sport feels fantastic to play, and I continue to be astonished by just how responsive and accurate motion controls are here. Some of my highlights include: Table Tennis, which added more strategy and depth with enhanced spin and curve mechanics; Skateboarding, which uses the Switch 2’s mouse controls to great effect for fast-paced racing and explorative segments; and Thumb Wrestling, which somehow made something seemingly mundane feel highly satisfying and exciting to play. I have a few gripes, mainly the removal of Football (or Soccer) and Chambara at launch, but I’m hoping they’ll be added down the line through some sort of update or DLC. If you want a simple yet exhilarating game to play with family and friends during the upcoming holiday season, this is easily my top recommendation. I have to say that I was a bit skeptical about Splatoon Raiders when it was first shown off. I’ve been playing Splatoon since the original dropped on Wii U (yes, I was one of the five people who bought one), and the idea of pivoting away from the iconic Turf War into a more single-player-oriented experience felt like a bold move. But boy, did it pay off. In our glowing five-star Splatoon Raiders review, we called it “a wonderful solo reinvention of the popular multiplayer series filled with smartly designed missions and endlessly engaging progression systems”. This third-person looter shooter is jam-packed with content; there’s a vast array of missions to run through with various difficulty levels, more than a hundred weapons to choose from, and even an online co-op mode including gear, weapon parts, and more. Pair that with a stellar progression system, stunning visuals, and intelligent level design, and you’re looking at an exceptional Switch 2 experience. I think it’s fair to say that Pokémon Pokopia is the biggest surprise hit of 2026. Of course, the Pokémon name itself is always going to entice a number of players, but not many could’ve foreseen the universal acclaim and social media attention that this spinoff would receive. In fact, Pokopia proved to be such a phenomenon that there were global shortages of the physical edition of the game that even affected me personally. But when I did get my mitts on Pokémon Pokopia, it gripped me in a way that no ‘cosy’ game has managed to do since my time with Animal Crossing: New Leaf back in 2013. And, in my view, Pokopia takes the Animal Crossing formula and dials it up to 11. You’ve still got that core duty to assist your fellow villagers by building homes, upgrading infrastructure, and sprucing up your locality, but the individual Pokémon feel so much more distinct and charismatic than Animal Crossing’s residents, and the sheer scale of the world is something to behold. The main story also has a surprisingly dark tone to it, as you take control of Ditto to investigate humanity's disappearance. You can spend hundreds of hours in Pokopia building fancy custom houses, filling out the Pokédex, or just interacting with your favorite pocket monsters — it’s the perfect game to relax and unwind with, and now there are even new DLC areas to explore, which we’ve loved so far. Pokémon Pokopia is the highest-rated Pokémon title in history according to Metacritic, and while I’d personally put a couple of mainline entries ahead of it, I really couldn’t recommend the game enough. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is my most-played game of 2026. I racked up more than 200 hours for my review, and to say it had me hooked would be an understatement. For me, this is the best game the series has produced thus far, with staggering scale, excellent tactical combat, a mesmerizing cast, and a stellar soundtrack to match. In Fortune’s Weave, you take control of four heroes, known as the Flame Lords, in their mission to win the Heroic Games, and have a wish granted by Divine Sovereign Solel. However, an impending threat is on the horizon, with the land of Dagda thrust into turmoil after the demonic god Balor sews disorder. Being able to play as all of the Flame Lords and experience their interwoven stories one by one was an absolute joy. Seeing each unique yet interconnected story unfold, recruiting allies, and building the ultimate units has never felt so satisfying, and it all builds to an epic conclusion which makes the time investment feel genuinely rewarding. Dungeon sections add some welcome variation and keep the experience feeling well-paced; new mechanics like Blaze Arts add even more combat depth, and the map designs are brilliant right across the board (though they reach a real peak towards the back end of the game). The visual upgrade over Fire Emblem: Three Houses is also considerable, and performance is stable even in the busiest moments. If you played Three Houses and loved that, or if you’re just an RPG fan at all, I think Fortune’s Weave is a true must-play — it's easily among the best Switch 2 games you can play today, and I firmly stand by the perfect five-star score I bestowed upon it. You saw this coming, right? The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is an all-time great of gaming, and the Switch 2 remake is pretty much flawless. Ocarina of Time is a true masterclass in design. A combination of expertly composed music, distinctly crafted domains, and legendary characters helps to imprint a memory of each area you explore in the mind for eternity. Dungeons are exceptionally varied, filled with fun puzzles and grandiose boss battles. And the narrative, though simple, is executed fantastically as the Hero of Time ventures through the world of Hyrule both as a child and as a young adult. The remake, while staying very faithful to the source material, adds some excellent quality-of-life changes that make the game far more palatable for modern audiences. Manual jumping, button-mapped items, free camera control, and roll-to-sprint make the adventure feel a whole lot smoother. Combat feels far snappier and more impactful too, with steadier movement helping you feel in control during skirmishes. And the visual reimagining is sensational too — the lighting, the character models, the small details… they all add up to something magical. And you also get a near frame-perfect 60fps gameplay experience here as well — I barely noticed a single drop during my entire playthrough. As relentless as the flow of time may be, our love for Ocarina of Time is unchanged. As our reviewer, Josephine Watson, said: “Whether you’re an adult or a child, when you boot up the remake, it’s not a game you’ll forget in a hurry”.

item.title: SALES: Samsung's 1TB 990 SSD drops to 19 cents per GB amid the memory crisis — grab it for $40 off
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Getting your hands on fast NVMe storage for your PC or laptop has become extremely challenging. That said, the Samsung 990 SSD is currently available at a discounted price of $189.99, against its original list price of $229.99 on Amazon. Although the $40 saving might not seem that impressive, deals on high-performance internal SSDs are becoming harder to come by amid the ongoing NAND and DRAM crisis. If you've been holding off on a storage upgrade, this could be a good opportunity to pick up a reliable, high-speed SSD. The Samsung 990 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that uses Samsung's latest V9 QLC NAND flash memory and a DRAM-less controller. It was introduced earlier this year with MSRPs of $269.99 for the 1TB model and $529.99 for the 2TB model. The 1TB model offers sequential read and write speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and 6,450 MB/s, making it an excellent option for everyday computing, gaming, and handling large files. Samsung rates the drive for up to 400TB of written data, although it offers just three years of warranty. It features a single-sided M.2 2280 design, which should make it compatible with a wide range of desktop motherboards, laptops, and even mini-PCs. Samsung's 990 is rated for read speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and write speeds of up to 6,450 MB/s, offering plenty of bandwidth for modern games, large files, and everyday applications. In our testing of the 2TB variant, we found that the Samsung 990 delivers reasonably good all-around performance, particularly for gaming and everyday applications. It offered similar performance to the Samsung 990 EVO Plus in some tests. However, it fell behind competing drives such as the Crucial P310 and WD Blue SN5100 in others, particularly during file transfers. One of its biggest advantages is its large write cache, which allows it to maintain speeds of nearly 6,100 MB/s for more than 57 seconds before performance drops once the cache is exhausted. Its power efficiency may not be the best, but overall it is a competent budget PCIe 4.0 SSD. For anyone upgrading from an older SATA SSD or a traditional hard drive, the Samsung 990 should offer a noticeable improvement in boot times, application loading, and overall system responsiveness. At its current price of $189.99, it is also a suitable option for expanding game storage without spending a fortune.

item.title: SALES: 12 fabulous gifts inspired by some of my favorite destinations and hotels
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
I’m on the road about half the year on assignment for TPG and on any given week, you might find me browsing the jade market in Taipei, window-shopping through Galerie Vivienne in Paris or strolling through the San Telmo market in Buenos Aires on the hunt for collectibles. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve seen a souvenir, piece of art, sweet treat or other little curio and thought, “Wouldn’t this make a great gift for so and so?” The only trouble is, I travel light, so there’s nary a nook or cranny in my carry-on to fit a gift, let alone several. I do, however, make a mental inventory of potential gifts I see so that I can order them for friends and family later. Here are a few of my favorite recent finds that might be perfect for someone on your holiday gift list, all inspired by my travels. Best for: Armchair travelers who like to keep cozy There’s a lot I love about 1 Hotels — their sustainable ethos, the Bamford bath amenities, in-room filtered water taps, the smattering of hyperlocal, destination-specific activities on offer to guests, bustling public spaces with unique dining concepts and…the bathrobes. I’m not usually a bathrobe kind of guy, but I can’t resist donning one of these ultracomfortable numbers anytime I’m a guest at one of these properties. Simple and soft, with a gray jersey-knit lining and a loose hoodie, they’re perfect for lounging with a cappuccino while you try to stave off jet lag. TPG tip: You might want to make this purchase at an actual 1 Hotel boutique so you can earn more points per dollar with a credit card that offers a travel or hotel category bonus. Best for: The Japanophile you want to impress Like an unstoppable force meeting an immovable object, my delight in purchasing travel souvenirs is only impeded by the limited space in my small city apartment. That’s why I love the little lacquerware boxes and trays from Zohiko, a boutique in Kyoto’s Nakagyo Ward that traces its history back to the 17th century. I especially love the finely filigreed Kirikane style, where patterns or shapes are cut out in gold or silver leaf and pressed into place. I purchased a glossy black box with gold inlay of cherry blossoms and autumn leaves on my last visit, and I keep it on my nightstand to hold my wedding ring and watch. TPG tip: Make a trip to Japan out of it and browse the physical Zohiko boutique (you can also enjoy tax-free purchases if you’re visiting) while checking out some of Kyoto’s exciting new hotels. Best for: Folks who appreciate colorful, culturally significant crafts Inevitably, every time I’m traipsing around Bogotá, I find myself drawn to this gorgeous little boutique in the city’s upscale Chapinero neighborhood, which sources fair-trade handcrafted pieces of art and decor from small communities around the country, including woven baskets starting at just $18. I am personally drawn to carefully carved wooden Tamo bowls from the coastal Nariño region, decorated with brightly dyed strands of wheat or barley fiber, but you can find everything from woven baskets to hammocks, jewelry and even pieces of furniture. TPG tip: While you can often haggle for handicrafts in Colombia, prices in this boutique are as marked, so save your negotiating skills for street vendors. Best for: Helping a friend spruce up their interior decor game Although long popular with backpackers and river cruisers, Luang Prabang still feels like an under-the-radar find in mountainous Laos, sitting on the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan Rivers. It’s also a hotbed of fair-trade arts and crafts. A standout atelier in town is Ock Pop Tok, an art school, store and restaurant that aims to revive, support and teach traditional Lao artistic techniques. Visitors can take classes in silk-weaving, batik-dyeing and embroidery, among other offerings. I am always tempted to buy out the textile section of the boutique, but I usually limit myself to a vibrant wall hanging or two. TPG tip: Don’t just make a purchase; spend a few days as a student at Ock Pop Tok to pick up a new craft yourself. Officina Profumo Farmaceutica Santa Maria Novella Best for: Travelers who like their perfumes with a hint of historical luxury Of course, I’d suggest visiting the original Florence flagship of this bath and beauty purveyor, which dates back to 1221. It feels a little like visiting Ollivanders Wand Shop from “Harry Potter,” with antique cases bursting with all-natural unguents and elixirs whose formulas were originally developed by Dominican friars. But if you can’t get there, there are also locations around the U.S., including those in West Hollywood, California, Soho in New York City and Bal Harbour, Florida. I tend to keep it simple and go for the pure sweet almond oil, but you could also go regal and buy a bottle of the perfumery’s citrusy Acqua della Regina, created for Catherine de' Medici as a gift for her husband, the future king of France, back in 1533. TPG tip: It can sometimes be less expensive to purchase these products from the original store in Florence, so why not make a trip out of it? Best for: The fashionable cowboys at your rodeo I love an eye-catching accessory, and belts are my statement pieces of choice. So on my last visit to Buenos Aires, I stopped by Arandu Talabarteria’s tony boutique in Recoleta. The whole store is inspired by a romanticized version of gaucho life on the pampas. You can find sturdy leather boots, billowy bombacha pants, cozy ponchos and my favorite: woven belts with intricate threadwork and high-quality leather. They start at $45 and can range into the hundreds of dollars, depending on the level of detail and craftsmanship. Best of all, you can ship to the U.S., so you don’t have to cross the equator to stock up. TPG tip: They also have dog collars for your faithful canine companion. Best for: The high-flying #avgeek in your life If you’ve followed me for the past few years, you know I’m pretty much obsessed with KLM’s tile Delft houses, the little replicas of actual historical buildings around the Netherlands that the airline hands out to long-haul business-class passengers. I’ve attended the unveiling of each year’s new house for several years now, and my own collection has grown into a veritable village. If you have an equally #avgeeky member of your gifting circle and are looking for the perfect present, then you might want to consider buying one of these beauties for them. Historian Mark Zegeling’s “Little Kingdom by the Sea” book set, which delves into the history of all 107 of the houses, is a great accompanying gift as well. TPG tip: Be sure to use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees so you don’t get dinged with a 1-3% surcharge when buying your house. Best for: Swanky sunseekers who want to make a splash How do you tell me you summer on the French Riviera without telling me you summer on the French Riviera? You simply tote around a sunshiney yellow-and-white-striped beach bag from the iconic Carlton Cannes, the first luxury hotel to open in the city, way back in 1911. A lot has changed since then, but the simple design is meant to evoke the Côte d’Azur of yore, when you might have found Cary Grant and Grace Kelly sunbathing on the plage between scenes of “To Catch a Thief.” TPG tip: Make your purchase in person and use an IHG One Rewards credit card to earn multiple points per dollar. Singapore Sling glass from Raffles Singapore Best for: International imbibers with a sweet tooth You might find it hard to remember your visit to Singapore, let alone pick up some souvenirs as gifts for friends, after you’ve had a few Singapore Slings at the Raffles Hotel’s iconic Long Bar. That’s why it might come in handy to pick up a keepsake Singapore Sling glass for your friends from the hotel’s online boutique. It’s like taking a sip of history with you. The nation’s signature drink was invented by Ngiam Tong Boon back in 1915 and is an intoxicating (and sweet!) mix of gin, grenadine, cherry liqueur, Benedictine, Curacao and both pineapple and lime juice. Even a sip can transport you back to a sultry Southeast Asian evening. TPG tip: Pick a card that earns bonus rewards on everyday purchases, like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so you’re making the most of your spending. Best for: Your friends’ (or your own) globe-trotting tots We can’t forget about the kids! In my experience, there are few better or more engaging (or educational) ways to get the tykes in your life interested in travel than Little Passports, a subscription membership where each month, your child is mailed a new box focusing on individual countries, animals, crafts and even DIY science experiments, depending on their specific subscription and age. TPG tip: Don’t forget to choose the subscription length you want from the start, otherwise, these charges might sneak up on you month after month if you don’t cancel. Officine Universelle Buly combs and creams Best for: Your favorite skincare aficionado I first came across Officine Universelle Buly’s sweet-smelling body products during a stay at the Rosewood Hotel de Crillon in Paris last year, and I promptly swiped several tubes of shampoo, conditioner and body lotion from my suite to use at home. On my next visit to the City of Light, though, I stopped by the enchanting store in the 6th arrondissement to sniff through various scents and balms tinged with exotic notes like Madagascar amber and Maltese iris. They also have fabulous tortoiseshell hair clips and combs that you can have monogrammed for even the most discerningly coiffed companions in your life. TPG tip: If you’re purchasing liquid products and not checking a bag, make sure they comply with carry-on limits. Best for: Yourself! This is the ultimate self-care splurge In recent years, more and more hotel chains have started selling the mattresses they use directly to customers. And while you might be a Westin Heavenly Bed fan, or perhaps a devotee of DoubleTree’s signature Sweet Dreams mattress, I personally recommend a Four Seasons mattress, which has the plushest pillowtop of any hotel bed I’ve experienced. After staying at dozens of Four Seasons over the years, I finally took the plunge and purchased one for myself about six years ago and I’ve never slept better. It’s definitely a splurge, but you can’t put a price tag on a great night’s sleep. So make this one a gift for yourself. TPG tip: Given the price tag, wait until you have a new credit card with a minimum spending requirement to meet to earn its welcome offer so you can put your splurge to good use.

item.title: SALES: 15 prettiest places to go for a winter break in the UK
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Some people dream of faraway travels to sandy beaches or snow-covered winter wonderlands, but there is something special about a winter holiday in the UK – no long flights, no visas, no need to pack for a lengthy journey, just the chance to switch off and relax. I firmly believe that a winter holiday in the UK can be the ultimate way to recharge. Cosy evenings by roaring fires, cold pints of craft ale in the corners of historic pubs, long walks through the glorious countryside on crisp, sunny mornings after hearty breakfasts, but also exciting winter city breaks, beach walks and wonderfully scenic hikes. In the lead-up to Christmas, our favourite hotels across the country deck the halls with mistletoe and glittering decorations, while animated chatter spills out of restaurants as guests reunite with old friends. Come January, things slow down, with indulgent spa sessions enjoyed after long walks along wild stretches of our spectacular coastline or visits to Sunday farmers' markets. Whether you're planning a long weekend exploring the Christmas markets of Manchester and Birmingham, a romantic escape to the Scottish Highlands or a few peaceful days by the sea, there's no shortage of places to discover during the colder months. From cosy countryside retreats to exciting winter city breaks, these are the best places to go for a winter holiday in the UK this year, with tried-and-tested recommendations of what to do, where to eat and where to stay. Where is the best place to go on a winter break in the UK? The best place for a winter break in the UK depends on the kind of holiday you're after and where you are based. For dramatic landscapes, cosy hotels and scenic walks, the Scottish Highlands and the Lake District are hard to beat, while the Cairngorms are ideal for those hoping to enjoy winter sports. If you prefer a city escape, Edinburgh, York and Bath offer a wonderful mix of history, cultural attractions and festive activities. For something a little quieter, the North Norfolk coast and the Isle of Wight are particularly lovely during the colder months, when the summer crowds have disappeared. Where is a good winter city break? Some of the best winter city breaks in the UK include Edinburgh, York, Bath and Manchester. Edinburgh is particularly magical in the lead-up to Christmas, with festive markets, seasonal attractions and the imposing Edinburgh Castle overlooking the city. York is another excellent choice, with its medieval streets, independent shops and magnificent York Minster, while Bath is ideal for a romantic long weekend exploring its Georgian architecture and thermal spa. Manchester and Birmingham are also great options for Christmas shopping, lively restaurants and cultural attractions. Further afield, European cities such as Paris, Berlin, Budapest and Kraków make wonderful winter city breaks. Where can I find cheap winter breaks in the UK? Some of the best places for cheap winter breaks in the UK are seaside towns, smaller cities and countryside destinations where accommodation prices tend to drop outside the peak tourist season. Margate, the North Norfolk coast and parts of the Isle of Wight can offer good-value stays during the quieter winter months, while cities such as York, Manchester and Birmingham are worth considering for an affordable long weekend. For the best deals, travel midweek, avoid Christmas and New Year, and look for hotel offers. Booking in advance can also help keep costs down.

item.title: SALES: Top Destinations in North America, Mexico, and the Caribbean for 2027
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK, Condé Nast Traveler
Travel choices in 2027 are shaped by a mix of personal inspiration, cultural shifts, and evolving sustainability priorities. From the turquoise waters of Jamaica’s South Coast to the high-altitude adventures of New Mexico, the year’s best destinations reflect a growing emphasis on meaningful travel experiences. In the wake of Hurricane Melissa, Jamaica’s South Coast offers opportunities to support local recovery efforts while enjoying farm-to-table dining and design-forward boutique stays. Meanwhile, Curaçao, a culturally rich island, is gaining attention as a FIFA World Cup destination, with new flights and resorts highlighting its vibrant on-the-ground energy. These destinations are not only places to visit but also reflections of broader trends in travel, such as cultural engagement and environmental responsibility. In Canada’s British Columbia, Clayoquot Sound remains a secluded wilderness area, now offering Indigenous-owned hospitality that deepens the connection between visitors and the land. The Ahousaht First Nation’s Wahous Wilderness Lodge, opening in July 2026, is a landmark in this shift. Located in Quait Bay, the 16-room floating lodge and four forest cabins were reacquired by the Nation’s hereditary chiefs through the Maaqutusiis Hahoulthee Stewardship Society in 2022. Guests are welcomed with tide-to-table dining, a shoreline spa, and a ceremonial welcome in the cedar longhouse, culminating in a traditional salmon barbecue that blends food, storytelling, and cultural exchange. The three-Michelin-star Clayoquot Wilderness Lodge, already a standout, is also evolving to align with these values. Beyond these highlights, Oregon’s Willamette Valley is merging its reputation for Pinot Noir with a sophisticated, sustainability-focused food scene, while Taos, New Mexico, is experiencing an arts and cultural renaissance against a backdrop of high-altitude adventure. Each destination on the list includes expert recommendations for accommodations, dining, and activities, providing a comprehensive guide for travelers seeking both inspiration and practical planning. As the year unfolds, these locations will continue to shape the narrative of travel, balancing exploration with a deeper understanding of the places we visit.
